title: De altitudine columnarum sub proprio pondere corruentium

deep.reconstruction:
The page completes the reformulation begun on p.166. Euler has just shown that the curves of the earlier sections (free top end A, base clamped or merely resting at an inflection point O) do not fit the real problem. In that problem both ends of the column stay on the same vertical line. He therefore lets the top end A carry an unknown horizontal reaction. Its size, he says, cannot be fixed in advance: it only comes out at the end of the calculation, being whatever force is needed to keep A on the vertical. In modern terms this is a statically indeterminate support reaction found together with the deflection.

He then widens the problem ('Status Quaestionis', a second §6; the numbering is duplicated in the print). Take a cylindrical column, or an elastic strip of the same stiffness, standing vertically along AB, with A and B fixed in position. At the midpoint C apply a small horizontal force Cc that bends it into a curve ACB differing only infinitesimally from the straight line AB. Find the shape of ACB under this force together with the column's own weight. Then ask whether the bent shape can persist as Cc tends to zero. If it can, the column has a non-trivial equilibrium shape arbitrarily close to the straight one with no lateral load. It therefore cannot resist even the least curvature, and collapses under its own weight.

This is the adjacent-equilibrium (neutral-equilibrium, bifurcation) criterion for buckling, reached by a perturbation method: add a small lateral load, solve the linearised problem, and find the parameter values at which the response no longer needs the load. Here the parameter is the critical height or weight.

§7 announces that the problem is hard. Euler therefore starts with the simplest case, a discrete model: two rigid half-columns joined at C by an elastic hinge with a fixed resisting moment. The next page develops it with weights M, angle θ, a spring moment 2Eeθ, and CO = a sinθ. This is a one-degree-of-freedom rigid-link model of buckling under distributed self-weight.
errors: No mathematical error on this page; it is purely programmatic.
The section number §6 is printed twice (once on p.166 and again here under 'Status Quaestionis'). This is a numbering slip in the original.

Physically, how the top support A shares the vertical load is left unstated here; only a horizontal reaction is introduced. That is a modelling choice rather than an error. Whether Euler's final result for this pinned-pinned self-weight case is correct is debated in the literature (Truesdell's commentary), but I am unsure of the details and nothing on this page decides it.

ideas.what: Buckling under self-weight found as the limit in which a deflection caused by a vanishing lateral force persists.
ideas.modern_name: Adjacent-equilibrium / bifurcation criterion via a lateral perturbation (imperfection) approach
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (1744 elastica; 1757 and 1778 column papers); later formalised by Bryan, Southwell and others
ideas.where_published: E65 Additamentum De curvis elasticis (1744), E238, E508–E510 (1778)

ideas.what: The horizontal reaction at the constrained top end is unknown and is determined by the solution itself.
Replace the continuous column by two rigid bars with an elastic hinge to solve the simplest case first.
ideas.usually_credited_to: Common in later stability theory; Euler used such models in his 1770s column papers

deep.surprise_reason: This is a programmatic page restating the problem and the perturbation and limit strategy, then introducing the rigid-link model. All of it is known from Euler's column papers and is discussed in Truesdell's history of elasticity.
transcription_corrections: The transcription is essentially faithful to the image.
'figura incuruata A B C' is as printed, although the curve is called 'A C B' elsewhere.
The marginal note 'Tab. IV. Fig. 4.' sits beside the first lines of the second §6.
